questions.title: The General's Question
questions.storyContext: Briefing room, SAFTI Military Institute. Your report is done — two weeks of analysis from mountains of data. The Chief picks up your executive summary, reads it, puts it down. "My commanders were making decisions on positions that were twenty minutes old. Before that, the screen crashed at 500 users. Before that, we couldn't get signal in half the training area." He looks at each of you. "Was this a technology problem, a design problem, or a people problem?"
questions.facilitatorPrompt: He's looking at all of us. What actually caused the stale data? Was it the jungle network? The system not built for failure? Or commanders who were never trained to question what the screen was showing them?

options.label: Network problem, sir. Dead zones we couldn't fully solve. Data got stuck in transit. Invest in portable relay equipment and satellite backup for every exercise, and the data arrives on time.
Design problem, sir. When data was stale, the system showed it as if it were fresh — no timestamp, no warning. It should have flagged it instead of pretending everything was fine.
Doctrine problem, sir. Commanders trusted the screen like a map. But screens can be wrong. Train every officer to cross-reference digital info with radio reports and their own eyes.
Honestly sir, all three. Network unreliable, software didn't handle it gracefully, commanders weren't trained to question it. We have a phased plan — but it takes three years and significant budget.

questions.title: The Next Generation
questions.storyContext: The Chief nods. Then: "Tell me something bigger. We're building a new generation of soldiers who fight in a world that's as much digital as physical. I can fast-track one capability into the SAF's training roadmap for the next five years. Every recruit and officer will be shaped by what you recommend. What should it be?"
questions.facilitatorPrompt: This shapes the next generation of the SAF. What was the hardest thing we faced during Northstar — not just the technical problems? What capability, if our people had it, would have changed the outcome?

options.label: Battlefield AI, sir. Specialists who deploy AI systems in the field — machines that learn from live data and suggest tactical options in real time. It's where warfare is heading.
People who understand both the digital and the physical, sir. Right now tech teams don't think about terrain and field commanders don't think about data. Train specialists who live in both worlds.
Resilient communications, sir. Everything fell apart the moment the network dropped. Portable relays, satellite fallback, manual radio procedures. Without comms, nothing else we build matters.

Data literacy across every rank, sir. From private to general, everyone learns to read, question, and act on digital information. The stale data crisis happened because commanders trusted a screen they didn't understand.
